summary: Describes how Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers could be implemented on 802.11 wireless links. Fast handovers aim to reduce the interruption when a mobile device moves from one access point's network to another. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a device moves from one wireless access point to another, it briefly cannot send or receive data. RFC 4260 describes how the Mobile IPv6 fast handover protocol can shorten that gap on 802.11 networks, using information from the radio layer to start the IP work before the move is finished.

questions: how does fast handover work on 802.11
subtitle: Applying the Mobile IPv6 fast handover protocol to WiFi networks, and the price of finding the new access point.

tldr.problem: A device that moves between wireless access points loses the ability to send and receive packets until it registers a new address, which is too long an interruption for live traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Fast handover uses link-layer information about nearby access points to start the IP work early: the device tells the old access router where it is going, the two access routers set up a tunnel, and traffic is forwarded to the new router before the device has finished moving.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document. It applies the protocol of RFC 4068 to 802.11 networks and works through three deployment scenarios, and it notes that the radio scan needed to find the new access point is itself the largest remaining delay.

facts.label: Relay deployment layout
facts.value: Two IP subnets, three access routers and five access points each

today: RFC 4260 is an Informational document from November 2005 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It applies the fast handover protocol specified in RFC 4068 to 802.11 networks and works through three deployment scenarios; the protocol itself is defined in RFC 4068, not here.

sections.title: Why a Fast Handover Needs the Link Layer
sections.content:
The Mobile IPv6 Fast Handover protocol, specified in RFC 4068, has been proposed as a way to minimise the interruption in service that a Mobile IPv6 node experiences when it changes its point of attachment to the Internet. Without such a mechanism, a mobile node cannot send or receive packets from the time it disconnects from one point of attachment in one subnet until it registers a new care-of address from the new point of attachment in a new subnet. Such an interruption would be unacceptable for real-time services such as Voice over IP.

The basic idea behind a fast handover is to leverage information from the link-layer technology to either predict or rapidly respond to a handover event, so that IP connectivity is restored at the new point of attachment sooner than it otherwise would be. By tunnelling data between the old and new access routers, IP connectivity can be provided in advance of the actual Mobile IP registration with the home agent or the correspondent node. Real-time services are then re-established without waiting for that registration to complete, and because Mobile IP registration involves time-consuming Internet round-trips, the interruption is shorter than with an ordinary Mobile IP handover.

The information a link layer can supply, and the timing of its availability before, during or after a handover, differ according to the technology in use. This document gives deployment examples for Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers on 802.11 networks: an overview of the relevant parts of 802.11, an examination of how and when handover information might become available to the IP layers that implement fast handover, both in the network infrastructure and on the mobile node, and finally the protocol steps in that environment.
sections.plainLanguage: When a device moves from one wireless access point to another, it briefly cannot send or receive data. Fast handover shortens that gap by starting the IP work before the move is finished, so live traffic survives the change of network.

sections.title: Two Ways to Build an 802.11 Network
sections.content:
The document describes the two most likely relationships between access points, access routers and IP subnets in an 802.11 deployment, focusing on the infrastructure mode of 802.11. Usually a station is associated with one and only one access point at any instant, although implementations exist in which multiple associations per station are maintained as long as the access points are connected to disjoint distribution systems. A station may be in communication with an access point only when radio propagation conditions permit. As with any layer 2 technology, a handover from one layer 2 point of attachment to another does not necessarily mean a change of access router or subnet.

The first deployment, in Figure 1, has two IP subnets, each with three access routers and five access points. The access points act as link-layer relays, transporting Ethernet-layer frames between the wireless medium and the subnet. They do not generally implement any particular spanning tree algorithm, yet they forward only traffic addressed to stations known to be associated on a given access point. Each subnet sits on a single LAN or VLAN, and the example assumes the access points of subnet 2 cannot reach the VLAN on which subnet 1 is implemented. A handover from AP1 to AP2 therefore needs no change of access router, because all three access routers are link-layer reachable from a station connected to any of AP1 to AP5. Such handoffs would not require IP-layer mobility management, although some IP-layer signaling may be needed to establish that connectivity to the existing access router is still available. A handover from AP5 to AP6 does require a change of access router, and an IP-layer handover mechanism is needed for a low-interruption handover between them.

The second deployment, in Figure 2, integrates each access point with exactly one access router on a disjoint VLAN. Every change of access point then means a change of access router, so every handover needs an IP-layer handover mechanism to keep the interruption low. The access router shares a MAC-layer identifier with its attached access point.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two common ways to build the network. Either several access points share the same access routers, so moving between them changes nothing at the IP level, or every access point has its own access router, so every move changes the IP network and needs the fast handover machinery.

sections.title: The Steps of an 802.11 Handover
sections.content:
An 802.11 handover takes place when a station changes its association from one access point to another, which is called re-association. The process has seven steps, numbered 0 to 6. The station realises a handoff is necessary because of a degrading radio transmission environment for the current access point. It scans to see what access points are available, which produces a list of access points together with physical layer information such as signal strength. It chooses one of them and performs a join to synchronise its physical and MAC-layer timing parameters. It requests authentication with the new access point, which for an Open System is a single round-trip message exchange with null authentication. It then requests association or re-association, and a re-association request contains the MAC-layer address of the old access point while a plain association request does not. Under 802.11i the station and access point would execute 802.1X EAP-on-LAN procedures to authenticate the association. Finally the new access point sends a Layer 2 Update frame on the local LAN segment to update the learning tables of any connected Ethernet bridges.

There is no standardised trigger for the scan. It may be the result of decaying radio conditions on the current access point, or it may happen at other times set by local implementation decisions. Some network interface cards scan in the background, interleaving scans between data packets, which shortens the time needed to roam but puts a heavier burden on the access point, because the station typically places it in power-save mode before the scan and returns to the access point's channel afterwards to pick up queued packets. That can exhaust buffers on the access point and cause packet loss. Rate adjustment during the join, where the station chooses the best available transmission rate, can also be time-consuming and unpredictable.

In some 802.11 implementations the steps from the scan to the association are performed by firmware in rapid succession, and in those cases it may be impossible for the host to take any action, including sending or receiving IP packets, before the handover is complete. In other implementations the scan and the join can be invoked independently, which allows the scan to be performed far in advance of the handover. One study concluded that the 802.11 beacon scanning function may take several hundred milliseconds to complete, during which sending and receiving IP packets is not possible. Scanning too far in advance risks using out-of-date information: radio conditions may change so much that the target access point is no longer reachable and the join fails. Whether to scan early is therefore a policy question that each implementation has to consider carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: A station moves between access points in seven steps: notice the signal is bad, scan for other access points, join one, authenticate, associate, run the 802.1X checks, and update the switches. The scan is the slow part, because the radio cannot carry data while it is listening on every channel.

sections.title: The FMIPv6 Message Exchange
sections.content:
A fast handover nominally consists of seven messages. The mobile node sends a Router Solicitation for Proxy (RtSolPr) to find out about neighbouring access routers, and receives a Proxy Router Advertisement (PrRtAdv) containing one or more [AP-ID, AR-Info] tuples. It sends a Fast Binding Update (FBU) to the previous access router. The previous access router sends a Handover Initiate (HI) message to the new access router, which replies with a Handover Acknowledge (HAck). The previous access router sends a Fast Binding Acknowledgement (FBack) message to the mobile node on the new link, and optionally on the previous link if the FBU was sent from there. The mobile node then sends a Fast Neighbor Advertisement (FNA) to the new access router after attaching to it. If the handover is unanticipated, the mobile node may connect to the new access router before sending the FBU, in which case the FNA carries the FBU inside it and the remaining messages follow from there.

The document then traces three scenarios, each labelled by the sequence of events it contains, with numbered events from the 802.11 steps and lettered events from the message exchange. In the predictive scenario the host executes the scan before the handover and is able to send the FBU before it, so only the FNA is sent afterwards. This requires that the scan and join can be performed separately and under host control, which is possible in some implementations but not others. Steps 1 and 1a to 1b may run far in advance of the handover, which removes the scan from the critical path and lets one RtSolPr and PrRtAdv exchange complete so the host has link-layer information about some new access routers. The drawback is that a long interval between the scan and the handover leaves the FBU built on out-of-date information, and there is no guarantee the mobile node will attach to the desired access point, because radio conditions may change.

The reactive scenario needs no host intervention between the scan and the join, but it does require the mobile node to know the link-layer address of the new access router before the handover, so that it has a link-layer destination address for outgoing packets, which it then uses to send the FNA with the encapsulated FBU. The third scenario is completely reactive: the mobile node obtains no information about the new access router beforehand, solicits a router advertisement after the handover, and then sends an FNA with the encapsulated FBU immediately. That may be appropriate when the scan primitive is not available to the host, or when the wildcard form of the PrRtAdv returns too many results.
sections.plainLanguage: The handover is a short conversation between the device and the two access routers. The device asks the old router which routers are nearby, tells the old router where it is going, and the old router tells the new router to expect it. Traffic can then be tunnelled to the new router before the device has even finished moving.

sections.title: Beacon Scanning and Finding the New Access Router
sections.content:
The RtSolPr message is used to request information about the routers connected to one or more access points. The access points are named in the New Access Point Link-Layer Address option of the RtSolPr, and the associated IP-layer information is returned in the IP Address Option of the PrRtAdv. On an 802.11 link the link-layer address is the BSSID of an access point.

Beacon scanning produces the list of available access points along with signal strength information for each, and that list supplies the addresses for the options in the RtSolPr. The host obtains it by invoking the MLME-SCAN.request primitive, whose returned BSSIDs are the link-layer addresses of the available access points. Because beacon scanning takes on the order of a few hundred milliseconds to complete, and because it is generally not possible to send and receive IP packets during that time, the mobile node has to schedule these events with care so that they do not disrupt ongoing real-time services. The scan could be performed when the mobile node attaches to the network, before any real-time traffic starts.

If the interval between scanning and handover is too long, the neighbour list is out of date. Signal strengths of neighbouring access points may have changed dramatically, and a handover directed at the apparently best access point from the old list may fail. If the handover is executed in firmware, the station may even choose a new target access point that is entirely missing from the old list. Both cases limit the ability of the mobile node to choose the correct new access router for the FBU in an anticipated handover.

Aside from physical layer parameters such as signal strength, it may be possible to obtain all necessary information about neighbouring access points with the wildcard form of the RtSolPr, which makes the current access router return a list of neighbouring access points without interrupting communication with the current access point. Making that request when the mobile node first attaches, and periodically thereafter, would let it cache the [AP-ID, AR-Info] tuples and react more quickly when a handover becomes necessary. The catch is that the information does not include up-to-date signal strength, so it cannot be used to predict the next access point accurately. If an access router is attached to many access points, there may also be no room to list them all in the PrRtAdv. A more targeted approach, scanning only one or two channels of interest, would interrupt real-time traffic for much less time, but such optimisations are currently outside the scope of the 802.11 specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding the new access router starts with a radio scan that takes a few hundred milliseconds, during which no data can be sent. Scanning too early makes the list of nearby access points stale, and scanning too late puts the scan in the middle of the handover.

sections.title: What Has to Be Checked Before Traffic Moves
sections.content:
The security considerations applicable to fast handover are described in the base specification. In particular, the previous access router must be assured of the authenticity of the FBU before it begins to redirect user traffic. However, if the association with the new access point is not protected using mutual authentication, it may be possible for a rogue access point to fool the mobile node into sending an FBU when it is not in the mobile node's best interest. The Layer 2 Update frame of step 6 installs layer 2 forwarding state that can redirect user traffic, and can cause disruption of service if it is triggered by a malicious node.

Step 3, the request for authentication, could provide some security, but because of the identified weaknesses in WEP shared key security it should not be relied upon. Instead the Robust Security Network requires the station to undergo 802.1X Port-Based Network Access Control before proceeding to steps 5 or 6. 802.1X defines a way to encapsulate the Extensible Authentication Protocol on 802 networks, as EAPOL. With this method the client and access point take part in an EAP exchange that can itself encapsulate any of the various EAP authentication methods. The EAPOL exchange can output a Master Session Key and an Extended Master Session Key, from which transient keys are derived to encrypt and authenticate later traffic.

802.1X pre-authentication can be used between a station and a target access point while the station is still associated with another one, so authentication can be done in advance of the handover and service can resume faster after roaming. Because EAPOL frames carry only MAC-layer rather than IP-layer addresses, however, this is currently specified to work only within a single VLAN, where IP-layer handover mechanisms are not necessarily needed anyway. In the case that matters most for fast handover, roaming across subnet boundaries, the 802.1X exchange would have to be performed after the handover to the new access point, which adds handover delay while the exchange takes place and may involve round-trips to RADIUS or Diameter servers. The exchange could be avoided if a preexisting Pairwise Master Key is found between the station and the access point, which may be the case if the station has previously visited that access point, or one that shares a common back-end infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The old access router must check that the device really asked to be moved before it redirects traffic, or a fake access point could use the move to capture the traffic. The 802.11 security rules handle this with 802.1X, but doing that check across subnets happens after the move, which adds to the delay.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN 802.11 HANDOVER STEPS, AS LISTED IN THE RFC

data.title: An 802.11 handover
data.code:
0. The STA realizes that a handoff is necessary due to degrading
   radio transmission environment for the current AP.
1. The STA performs a scan to see what APs are available.
2. The STA chooses one of the APs and performs a join to
   synchronize its physical and MAC-layer timing parameters.
3. The STA requests authentication with the new AP.
4. The STA requests association or re-association with the new AP.
5. If operating in accordance with 802.11i, the STA and AP would
   execute 802.1X EAP-on-LAN procedures.
6. The new AP sends a Layer 2 Update frame on the local LAN segment.
